summaries.gardner: Berkshire Hathaway is the opposite of a Rule Breaker: a mature conglomerate in insurance, rail, utilities and manufacturing rather than the first mover in an emerging industry. It has a strong brand and well-known leadership, but its shares rose only about 6% over the past year versus about 20% for the S&P 500, and few commentators call it overvalued.
summaries.buffett: Berkshire is built on Buffett's own tenets: understandable businesses such as GEICO, BNSF and regulated utilities, owner-oriented management, a fortress balance sheet (about $365B of cash and Treasuries in mid-2026) and a per-share market value that compounded about 19.7% a year from 1965 to 2025. The open questions are whether Greg Abel, CEO since January 2026, can keep allocating capital as well, and whether its huge size limits future returns.
summaries.munger: Munger helped shape Berkshire as a collection of good businesses bought at fair prices and run with integrity, a model that fits his framework closely. Inverting the problem, its main risks are the loss of Buffett's capital-allocation judgment, very large catastrophe losses and its sheer size, but its conservative finances make permanent failure unlikely.
summaries.lynch: Lynch would class Berkshire as a stalwart: a large, steady company that grows with the economy and is best bought when cheap. At about 13 times trailing earnings and 1.5 times book value it is reasonably priced, but GAAP earnings swing with investment gains and growth is modest, so it is not a ten-bagger candidate.
summaries.fisher: Berkshire scores well on Fisher's points about management integrity, long-term outlook and conservative accounting, but poorly on research and development and on developing new products, because it is a holding company that grows mainly by acquisition. Its operating businesses are solid rather than innovation-led.
summaries.graham: Berkshire passes several of Graham's defensive tests: it is very large, has a strong balance sheet, EPS has more than tripled since 2015, and it trades at about 13 times average 2023-2025 earnings with P/E times P/B near 19. It fails on dividends, having paid none since 1967, and on uninterrupted profits, after a GAAP net loss in 2022 caused by unrealised investment losses.
summaries.thiel: Thiel's seven questions are aimed at new technology ventures, which Berkshire is not: it has no proprietary technology ten times better than rivals and grows through acquisitions in mature industries. It does score well on durability, a strong team and a unique, hard-to-copy position as the preferred permanent buyer of family businesses.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner focuses on durable growth at a fair price; Berkshire offers durability, low leverage at the parent and a modest valuation (about 13 times trailing earnings), but little exposure to the AI and cloud platform shifts he emphasises beyond its Apple and Alphabet holdings. Revenue was flat at $371.4B in 2025.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller seeks accelerating earnings and catalysts; Berkshire's operating earnings fell to $44.5B in 2025 before rising 16% to $13.0B in Q2 2026, and its stock has lagged the market over the past year. It is a defensive holding rather than the kind of high-conviction, momentum-driven bet he favours.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith wants high returns on capital, cash conversion and growth at a fair price; Berkshire's return on equity of about 12% and modest growth fall short of the asset-light compounders Fundsmith owns. Its many capital-intensive businesses (rail, utilities) do not fit his preference for high-margin, low-capital companies.
summaries.greenblatt: On a Magic Formula screen Berkshire looks attractive on earnings yield (EV/EBIT of about 7.5) and acceptable on return on capital (ROIC about 19%), though both figures are flattered by investment gains. Greenblatt's formula also excludes financial companies such as insurers, so it would normally not include Berkshire.
summaries.akre: Berkshire fits Akre's three-legged stool well on the first two legs: durable businesses and honest, owner-oriented managers with a 60-year record. The third leg, reinvesting at high returns, is weaker because its size and $360B-plus cash pile make it hard to find enough large, attractive investments.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai has often praised Berkshire, and it fits his low-risk emphasis: a huge cash cushion, low parent-company debt and stable businesses make permanent loss unlikely. But at about 1.5 times book value it is not a deep-discount Dhandho bet, so the upside is moderate.
summaries.wood: Berkshire does not fit Cathie Wood's disruptive-innovation framework: it owns insurance, railroads, utilities and manufacturers rather than leaders in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or genomic sequencing. Its exposure to those themes comes only indirectly through stock holdings such as Apple and Alphabet.
summaries.ackman: Berkshire matches much of Ackman's checklist: simple, predictable, cash-generative businesses, a fortress balance sheet, durable moats in BNSF and its utilities, and owner-minded management. The weaker points are modest growth and a price of about 1.5 times book, which is reasonable but not a large discount.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep admired Berkshire and owned it at Nomad, citing its 'scale economies shared' at GEICO, which keeps costs low and passes savings to customers. Today GEICO has lost share to Progressive, so the flywheel looks less strong than it did, though Berkshire's reputation as a permanent home for businesses still grows with time.
summaries.valentine: Valentine looked for young companies attacking large, painful problems with breakthrough products; Berkshire is a 60-year-old holding company in mature industries. It solves real needs (insurance, freight, power) but has none of the early-stage, product-driven traits he sought.
summaries.nash: Berkshire passes Tom Nash's safety tests easily, with $365.5B of cash and Treasuries against $128.6B of debt, positive free cash flow every quarter since early 2025 and a strong Loan Officer result. It fails his growth-focused steps: it is not tied to a secular trend like AI, trailing revenue grew 3.93%, its Rule of 40 score is about 10 and new CEO Greg Abel has led it only since January 2026. Nash's FCF-based DCF values it at about half the share price, though that method understates an insurer's float and investment portfolio.

momentum.evidence: BRK-B rose about 6.4% over the 52 weeks to October 13, 2026, versus about a 20.4% total return for the S&P 500 (SPY).

g4.evidence: Berkshire was built by Warren Buffett and is now run by Greg Abel (CEO since January 1, 2026), with Buffett remaining chairman and a famous long-term shareholder base.

g6.evidence: Commentators mostly describe the stock as fairly valued or cheap; at about 1.5 times book and 13 times trailing earnings, recent articles discuss the 'Buffett premium' leaking out rather than overvaluation.

simple.evidence: Its main businesses (GEICO auto insurance, BNSF railroad, regulated utilities, manufacturing and retail) are well described in its letters and easy for a careful generalist to understand, though insurance reserves add complexity.

b2.evidence: Per-share market value compounded about 19.7% a year from 1965 to 2025, and operating earnings rose from $21.9B in 2020 to $44.5B in 2025.

integrity.evidence: Berkshire publishes candid shareholder letters and an Owner's Manual, pays executives modestly with no stock options, and Greg Abel bought about $15M of shares in March 2026.

b6.evidence: Berkshire has held over $360B of cash rather than overpay for deals, and avoids fashionable acquisitions, though it did buy OxyChem in 2025.

roic.evidence: Return on equity is about 12% and ROIC about 19% on a trailing basis (StockAnalysis), with little parent-level debt, but much of the $129B of borrowings sits at BNSF and Berkshire Hathaway Energy.

fcf.evidence: Free cash flow was $25.0B in 2025, about 56% of the $44.5B of operating earnings, because BNSF and the utilities need heavy capital spending.

b10.evidence: Berkshire has retained all its earnings for decades, and its per-share market value grew about 19.7% a year from 1965 to 2025 versus 10.5% for the S&P 500.

safety.evidence: At about 1.49 times book value with $365B of cash and Treasuries, downside looks limited, but the price is not well below a conservative estimate of intrinsic value.

fairprice.evidence: About 13 times trailing earnings and 1.5 times book is a reasonable price for a high-quality, slow-growing conglomerate.

mu5.evidence: Its diversification across dozens of businesses, huge liquidity and conservative insurance underwriting leave few ways for the whole company to fail.

reinvest.evidence: BNSF and the utilities can absorb large investment, but its size means few opportunities can earn high returns, which is why cash exceeds $360B.

ly2.evidence: It is a classic stalwart: a large, diversified company whose earnings grow roughly with the economy.

ly3.evidence: The trailing P/E is about 13, while earnings growth has been uneven (EPS of $44.27, $41.27 and $31.04 per B-share equivalent for 2023-2025), so earnings growth is below the P/E.

runway.evidence: Revenue grew from $245.5B in 2020 to $371.4B in 2025 but was flat in 2025, and growth now depends mostly on acquisitions and GDP-like expansion.

ly7.evidence: Greg Abel bought about $15M of stock in March 2026 and Berkshire resumed buybacks on March 4, 2026 for the first time since May 2024, but the share count was roughly unchanged over the past year.

ly8.evidence: Berkshire is one of the most watched companies in the world, though sell-side analyst coverage is thin.

fi2.evidence: Berkshire adds new businesses through acquisitions (OxyChem in 2025) rather than developing new products itself.

fi3.evidence: Berkshire does not report a consolidated R&D figure, and research is not central to its model.

fi4.evidence: GEICO has a strong direct-selling model, but it lost market share to Progressive (about 14% to 12% of US auto premiums from 2020 to 2024).

longterm.evidence: Berkshire explicitly ignores quarterly results, keeps businesses forever and builds huge cash reserves for long-term opportunities.

gr1.evidence: Berkshire had $371.4B of revenue in 2025 and about $748B of shareholders' equity in mid-2026.

ni10.evidence: Berkshire reported a GAAP net loss of about $22.8B in 2022 because of unrealised investment losses, although its operating businesses were profitable.

gr4.evidence: Berkshire has paid no dividend since a single payment in 1967.

eps10.evidence: Net earnings per Class A share rose from $14,656 in 2015 to about $46,570 in 2025 ($66,968M over about 1.438M shares), more than tripling.

gr6.evidence: Average 2023-2025 EPS per B-share equivalent ($44.27, $41.27, $31.04) is about $38.86, so the $520.59 price is about 13.4 times average earnings.

gr7.evidence: A trailing P/E of about 13.0 times a P/B of about 1.49 gives roughly 19.4, below 22.5.

th1.evidence: Berkshire has no proprietary technology; its advantages are capital, reputation and scale.

timing.evidence: Higher interest rates have boosted income on its cash and float, and data-center power demand helps its utilities, but its businesses are not tied to a new technology wave.

th3.evidence: Berkshire grew from a failing textile mill into a diversified holding company by acquisitions, not by dominating a small market.

team.evidence: Buffett built one of the best long-term records in investing, and Greg Abel and Ajit Jain are widely regarded as highly capable operators.

th5.evidence: Its reputation brings owners of family businesses directly to it, and GEICO sells directly to millions of drivers.

durable.evidence: BNSF (one of two major western US railroads), regulated utilities and a $176B insurance float are long-lived assets unlikely to be made obsolete in 10-20 years.

th7.evidence: Its model of permanent, decentralised ownership is distinctive and hard to copy, but its opportunities (insurance, rail, utilities) are well known to others.

trend.evidence: Berkshire is not a leading beneficiary of AI or cloud computing, apart from holdings such as Apple and Alphabet and rising utility power demand from data centers.

dr1.evidence: Operating earnings fell to $44.5B in 2025 but rose 16% to $13.0B in Q2 2026, while the forward P/E of about 22.8 implies lower GAAP earnings ahead.

dr2.evidence: Buybacks and the deployment of cash could improve per-share value, but softening reinsurance prices and catastrophe exposure make a clear improvement uncertain.

dr4.evidence: Higher interest rates raise income on its Treasury holdings and float, but falling rates would cut that income and the economy drives BNSF and its manufacturers.

dr6.evidence: Possible drivers include larger buybacks, a big acquisition using its cash and GEICO's margin recovery, though none is scheduled.

dr7.evidence: Its diversification and fortress balance sheet make it one of the few stocks investors commonly hold as a large core position.

gm.evidence: Berkshire does not report a consolidated gross margin because its revenue mixes insurance premiums, freight, utilities and goods.

fcfyield.evidence: Trailing free cash flow of $24.2B gives an FCF yield of about 2.2%, modest but backed by $365B of cash and Treasuries.

gb2.evidence: EV/EBIT is about 7.5, which looks high-yielding, but trailing operating income includes investment gains; on operating earnings alone the yield is lower.

pa2.evidence: The CEO transition and GEICO's share loss may weigh on sentiment temporarily, but the business is not in a deep setback.

pa4.evidence: With about $365B of cash and Treasuries, $748B of equity and little parent-level debt, the risk of permanent loss is small.

wo1.evidence: Berkshire is not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing.

wo2.evidence: Its products (insurance, freight, power) do not show rapidly falling costs that unlock big new demand.

wo3.evidence: It owns no innovation platforms of the kind ARK tracks.

wo4.evidence: Its mature markets are not likely to grow many times larger in five years.

ac3.evidence: Investment income depends on interest rates, earnings on stock-market swings, and BNSF, energy and manufacturing on the economy and commodity prices.

ns1.evidence: GEICO's low-cost direct model historically passed savings to drivers, but it has lost ground to Progressive's telematics pricing.

ns4.evidence: Its balance sheet and reputation should keep it strong, but the shift from Buffett to Abel makes a clearly stronger position uncertain.

va2.evidence: It meets real needs such as insurance protection, freight transport and electricity, but it is not solving a new, painful problem with a breakthrough product.

tn1.evidence: Berkshire is a conglomerate of insurance, railroad, utilities and manufacturing businesses that is not built for a secular trend such as AI, apart from utility power demand from data centres and stakes such as Apple and Alphabet.

tn2.evidence: The market sees Berkshire as a diversified, cash-rich conglomerate run for steady compounding, and that is what it is; there is no large gap between story and reality.

tn3.evidence: It is a $1.1T US company with a long history, not a small cap, Chinese company, commodity producer, airline, seasonal business or startup.

tn4.evidence: It is profitable (trailing net income $85,768M) and has more cash ($365,514M) than debt ($128,599M), although revenue was flat in FY2025 ($371,444M vs $371,433M).

tn6.evidence: Trailing revenue grew 3.93% to $384,687M, and FY2025 growth was 0.00%.

tn11.evidence: Its parts are simple (insurance premiums, freight charges, regulated utility rates, product sales), but as a conglomerate it cannot be stated as one product that cures one pain for one customer group.

tn13.evidence: Scorecard total 80 of 130: cash vs debt 10, revenue growth 0, operating margin 5, short interest 10, institutional ownership (52.3%) 5, revenue faster than expenses 5, 5-year return (BRK-B +85.8% vs SPY's +91.1%) 5, moat 10, CEO 5, recession-proof pricing power 10, secular trend 0, culture and mission 10, talent 5.
